newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - British inflation jumps to two-year high.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - British inflation jumps to two-year high.

text.p: Headline British inflation leapt to 3.3 percent in the year to July, its highest rate in nearly two years, from 2.9 percent in June, the Office for National Statistics said on Tuesday.
Underlying retail price inflation, excluding volatile home loan payments, also jumped -- to 3.0 percent year-on-year from 2.7 percent in June, well above the government's 2.5 percent target.
Headline RPI was last higher in September 1995, when it was rattling along at 3.9 percent.
The financial markets were unfazed. The FTSE-100 share index shares was 40 points higher at 5,072 in afternoon trade. The pound was steady around 2.94 marks.

The government's Paymaster General, Geoffrey Robinson, said he expected to see underlying inflation back on target with in a couple of months as the full effects of Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's July 2 budget kick in.

The ONS said the climb in July inflation was largely due to one-off effects, notably a jump in petrol prices following budget duty increases and increased housing costs after a series of recent interest rate rises.
RPIY, which cuts mortgage payments and indirect taxes out of the inflation equation, fell 0.2 percent over the month and was just 2.2 up on a year ago.
"We tackled mortgage interest rates, we tackled the cost of petrol and of course it's the cost of petrol that...has given the increase we see at the moment," Robinson told BBC radio.

Petrol and oil prices rocketed by 14 percent in the year to July after Brown increased duty by four pence per litre. "Next month...we will get the benefit of the cut in VAT on fuel. We are confident we will see inflation coming down over the next few months, very much in line with the target we set," Robinson said.
The ONS said a cut in VAT on heating fuel, to five percent from eight, would feed into September's RPI.
But the main opposition Conservative Party blamed Tuesday's inflation rise squarely on Brown's budget.

"Labour's decision to jack up taxes...has fed straight through into higher prices," industry spokesman Michael Fallon said. "No wonder the Bank of England raise interest rates last week. They knew Brown had injected extra inflationary pressure into the system."

The Bank raised rates again last week in its ongoing quest to meet the government's inflation target two years out. That was the fourth quarter-point rise in as many months, taking base rates to seven percent.
The third of those increases was another source of inflationary pressure in July. Mortgage rates rose by an average 0.28 percentage points last month.

The Bank is worried that a flood of windfall payments to consumers from mutually-owned building societies converting into banks -- 35 billion pounds ($55.4 billion) in free shares at the last count -- will tip already-buoyant spending over into an inflationary boom. But perhaps not.

Sales data show consumers have spent their windfalls on goods like washing machines and televisions. But retailers have failed to crank up prices in response. Household goods prices fell 1.5 percent last month.

"There are still no signs of any meaningful upward pressure on prices," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets. "Consumers are still being very fussy about prices, even when spending their windfalls." ($ = 0.632 British Pounds)
